seo.title: Critical Security Mistakes ZK Engineers Make
seo.description: Learn from common security mistakes in zero-knowledge development. Avoid underconstrained circuits, faulty arithmetic, and verification bugs.

content.intro: ZK circuits are unforgiving. A single missing constraint can allow provers to generate valid proofs for false statements. Learn from these critical mistakes.

items.description: Signals that do not appear in any constraint let provers choose arbitrary values. This breaks the entire proof.
items.impact: Prover can generate valid proofs for any output regardless of actual inputs.
items.prevention: Audit every signal. Each must appear in at least one constraint or be derived from constrained values.
items.example: A public output signal that is assigned but never constrained to match the computation.

items.description: Treating a signal as boolean without constraining it to 0 or 1. Field elements have many other values.
items.impact: Prover can use non-boolean values, breaking conditional logic.
items.prevention: Always add `signal * (signal - 1) === 0` for any boolean signal.
items.example: A bit decomposition where each bit is not constrained to be 0 or 1.

items.description: Array lookups where the index is not constrained to valid range.
items.impact: Out-of-bounds access can leak information or cause unexpected behavior.
items.prevention: Add range checks for all array indices.
items.example: Merkle tree path index that could be any field element, not just 0 or 1.

items.description: Not constraining every step of Merkle path or getting left/right ordering wrong.
items.impact: Invalid proofs accepted. Non-existent leaves proven to exist.
items.prevention: Verify each hash step. Test with known roots.
items.example: Skipping the final hash comparison against the claimed root.

items.description: Assuming arithmetic works like integers. Field arithmetic wraps at the modulus.
items.impact: Large numbers wrap to small numbers. Comparisons break. Security assumptions fail.
items.prevention: Add range checks. Be explicit about field size assumptions.
items.example: Adding two large numbers expecting a larger result, but getting a small wrapped value.

items.description: Not checking that denominators are non-zero before division.
items.impact: Undefined behavior. Prover might be able to exploit edge cases.

items.description: Field elements have two square roots. Not specifying which one is expected.
items.impact: Prover can use either root, potentially breaking logic.
items.prevention: Constrain which square root by adding sign or range constraints.
items.example: Using sqrt in signature verification without constraining the sign.

items.description: Decomposing to bits but not constraining that bits reconstruct to original value.
items.impact: Bits do not represent the actual value. Proofs become meaningless.
items.prevention: Always add reconstruction constraint: sum of bits * powers of 2 == original.
items.example: Checking individual bits without verifying they sum to the original number.

items.description: Hash inputs that are not fully constrained allow hash manipulation.
items.impact: Prover can adjust unconstrained inputs to produce desired hash.
items.prevention: Every hash input must be fully constrained by circuit logic.
items.example: Hashing a message where part of the message is not constrained.

items.description: Verifying only part of a signature or not including the message.
items.impact: Signature forgery. Proofs for unauthorized actions.
items.prevention: Complete signature verification including message binding.
items.example: Checking signature math without including the signed message in the check.

items.description: Nullifiers that can be computed multiple ways for the same underlying item.
items.impact: Double-spending. Same asset used multiple times with different nullifiers.
items.prevention: Nullifier derivation must be deterministic and unique.
items.example: Nullifier = hash(secret) without including asset ID. Same secret, different assets.

items.description: Not validating that public keys are valid points on the curve.
items.impact: Invalid keys can cause signature verification to misbehave.
items.prevention: Validate all external curve points are on the correct curve and subgroup.
items.example: Accepting a public key without checking it's a valid elliptic curve point.

sections.heading: Setup and Verification Mistakes
sections.description: Errors in proof system setup and verification.

items.description: Using setup parameters generated by one party. That party can create fake proofs.
items.impact: Setup generator can forge proofs for any statement.
items.prevention: Use multi-party ceremonies (Powers of Tau) for trusted setup.
items.example: Generating proving/verification keys locally instead of using ceremony output.

items.description: Using the same proving key for different circuits.
items.impact: Proofs from one circuit might be valid for another, breaking security.
items.prevention: Each circuit requires its own setup. Never reuse keys.
items.example: Deploying multiple ZK applications with the same verification key.

items.description: Public inputs ordered differently between prover and verifier.
items.impact: Verification succeeds for wrong values. Proofs prove wrong things.
items.prevention: Strict public input ordering. Test prover/verifier integration.
items.example: Prover puts amount before address, verifier expects address before amount.

items.description: Proofs that can be replayed to repeat an action.
items.impact: Same proof used multiple times. Actions repeated unintentionally.
items.prevention: Include nonces, timestamps, or nullifiers in public inputs.
items.example: Proof for 'send 10 tokens' can be submitted multiple times.

sections.heading: Application Integration Mistakes
sections.description: Errors connecting ZK proofs to applications.

items.description: Proof proves something but does not specify what action it authorizes.
items.impact: Proof generated for one action used to authorize another.
items.prevention: Include action identifier in public inputs.
items.example: Proof of ownership used for both withdrawal and transfer.

items.description: Accepting proofs without recording their nullifiers.
items.prevention: Store all spent nullifiers. Check before accepting proofs.
items.example: Tornado Cash-style mixer without a nullifier set.

items.description: Accepting proofs from clients without validating the public inputs make sense.
items.impact: Malicious clients submit proofs with manipulated public inputs.
items.prevention: Validate public inputs server-side independent of the proof.
items.example: Client claims amount=1000000 in public inputs. Server trusts it.
